content: Hexokinase-1 (HK1) is an enzyme encoded by the HK1 gene located on chromosome 10 in humans. Hexokinases catalyze the phosphorylation of glucose to produce glucose-6-phosphate (G6P), which represents the first step in most glucose metabolism pathways. The HK1 gene encodes a ubiquitous form of hexokinase that is localized to the outer membrane of mitochondria. Mutations in this gene have been associated with hemolytic anemia caused by hexokinase deficiency. Alternative splicing of the HK1 gene results in five transcript variants encoding different isoforms, some of which are tissue-specific. Each isoform has a unique N-terminus, while the remainder of the protein is identical across all isoforms. A sixth transcript variant has been described, but it is not believed to encode a protein due to the presence of multiple stop codons. Structure HK1 is one of four highly homologous hexokinase isoforms found in mammalian cells. Gene The HK1 gene spans approximately 131 kilobases (kb) and consists of 25 exons. The first 5’ exon for the ubiquitously expressed HK1 isoform is located 85 kb downstream of exon R. Exon 7 encodes the porin-binding domain (PBD), which is conserved in mammalian HK1 genes. The remaining 17 exons are shared among all HK1 isoforms. In addition to exon R, a segment of the proximal promoter containing a GATA element, an SP1 site, a CCAAT box, and an Ets-binding motif is required for the expression of HK-R in erythroid cells. Protein The HK1 gene encodes a 100 kDa homodimer with a regulatory N-terminal domain (residues 1–475), a catalytic C-terminal domain (residues 476–917), and an alpha-helix connecting the two subunits. Both terminal domains consist of a large subdomain and a small subdomain. The flexible region of the C-terminal large subdomain (residues 766–810) can adopt various positions and is proposed to interact with the base of ATP. Glucose and G6P bind in close proximity at the Nand C-terminal domains, stabilizing a common conformational state of the C-terminal domain. One model suggests that G6P acts as an allosteric inhibitor by binding the N-terminal domain to stabilize its closed conformation, which in turn stabilizes a conformation of the C-terminal flexible subdomain that blocks ATP. Another model posits that G6P acts as an active inhibitor by stabilizing the closed conformation and competing with ATP for the C-terminal binding site. Studies suggest that the C-terminal domain is capable of both catalytic and regulatory functions. Meanwhile, the hydrophobic N-terminal domain lacks enzymatic activity but contains the G6P regulatory site and the PBD, which is responsible for the protein’s stability and binding to the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM). Function As one of two mitochondrial isoforms of hexokinase and a member of the sugar kinase family, HK1 catalyzes the rate-limiting and first obligatory step of glucose metabolism, which is the ATP-dependent phosphorylation of glucose to G6P. Physiological levels of G6P regulate this process by inhibiting HK1 through negative feedback, although inorganic phosphate (Pi) can relieve G6P inhibition. However, unlike HK2 and HK3, HK1 is not directly regulated by Pi, which aligns with its ubiquitous catabolic role. By phosphorylating glucose, HK1 effectively prevents glucose from leaving the cell and commits it to energy metabolism. Additionally, its localization and attachment to the OMM promote the coupling of glycolysis to mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, significantly enhancing ATP production by directly recycling mitochondrial ATP/ADP to meet the cell’s energy demands. Specifically, OMM-bound HK1 binds VDAC1 to trigger the opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore and release mitochondrial ATP to further fuel glycolysis. Another critical function of OMM-bound HK1 is cell survival and protection against oxidative damage. Activation of Akt kinase is mediated by HK1-VDAC1 coupling as part of the growth factor-mediated phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/Akt cell survival intracellular signaling pathway, thereby preventing cytochrome c release and subsequent apoptosis. Evidence suggests that VDAC binding by the anti-apoptotic HK1 and the pro-apoptotic creatine kinase are mutually exclusive, indicating that the absence of HK1 allows creatine kinase to bind and open VDAC. Furthermore, HK1 has demonstrated anti-apoptotic activity by antagonizing Bcl-2 proteins located at the OMM, which inhibits TNF-induced apoptosis. In the prefrontal cortex, HK1 putatively forms a protein complex with EAAT2, Na+/K+ ATPase, and aconitase, which functions to remove glutamate from the perisynaptic space and maintain low basal levels in the synaptic cleft. HK1 is the most ubiquitously expressed isoform among the four hexokinases and is constitutively expressed in most tissues, though it is predominantly found in the brain, kidney, and red blood cells (RBCs). Its high abundance in the retina, specifically in the photoreceptor inner segment, outer plexiform layer, inner nuclear layer, inner plexiform layer, and ganglion cell layer, underscores its crucial metabolic role. It is also expressed in cells derived from hematopoietic stem cells, such as RBCs, leukocytes, and platelets, as well as erythroid-progenitor cells. Notably, HK1 is the sole hexokinase isoform found in cells and tissues that rely heavily on glucose metabolism for their function, including the brain, erythrocytes, platelets, leukocytes, and fibroblasts. In rats, it is also the predominant hexokinase in fetal tissues, likely due to their constitutive glucose utilization. Clinical Significance Mutations in the HK1 gene are associated with type 4H of Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease, also known as Russe-type hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy (HMSNR). Due to the critical role of HK1 in glycolysis, hexokinase deficiency has been identified as a cause of erythroenzymopathies associated with hereditary non-spherocytic hemolytic anemia (HNSHA). Similarly, HK1 deficiency has resulted in cerebral white matter injury, malformations, psychomotor retardation, latent diabetes mellitus, and panmyelopathy. HK1 is highly expressed in cancers, and its anti-apoptotic effects have been observed in highly glycolytic hepatoma cells. Neurodegenerative Disorders HK1 may be causally linked to mood and psychotic disorders, including unipolar depression (UPD), bipolar disorder (BPD), and schizophrenia (SCHZ), through its roles in energy metabolism and cell survival. For instance, the accumulation of lactate in the brains of BPD and SCHZ patients may result from the decoupling of HK1 from the OMM, and by extension, glycolysis from mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. In SCHZ, decreased HK1 attachment to the OMM in the parietal cortex results in reduced glutamate reuptake capacity and glutamate spillover from synapses. The released glutamate activates extrasynaptic glutamate receptors, leading to altered structure and function of glutamate circuits, synaptic plasticity, frontal cortical dysfunction, and ultimately, the cognitive deficits characteristic of SCHZ. Similarly, HK1 mitochondrial detachment has been associated with hypothyroidism, which involves abnormal brain development and an increased risk for depression, while its attachment promotes neural growth. In Parkinson’s disease, HK1 detachment from VDAC via Parkin-mediated ubiquitylation and degradation disrupts the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (MPTP) on depolarized mitochondria, consequently blocking mitochondrial localization of Parkin and halting glycolysis. Further research is required to determine the relative HK1 detachment needed in various cell types for different psychiatric disorders. This research can also contribute to developing therapies targeting the causes of the detachment, from gene mutations to interference by factors such as beta-amyloid peptide and insulin. Retinitis Pigmentosa A heterozygous missense mutation in the HK1 gene (a change at position 847 from glutamate to lysine) has been linked to retinitis pigmentosa. Since this substitution mutation is located far from known functional sites and does not impair the enzyme’s glycolytic activity, it is likely that the mutation acts through another biological mechanism unique to the retina. Notably, studies in mouse retina reveal interactions between HK1, the mitochondrial metallochaperone Cox11, and the chaperone protein Ranbp2, which serve to maintain normal metabolism and function in the retina. Thus, the mutation may disrupt these interactions and lead to retinal degradation. Alternatively, this mutation may act through the enzyme’s anti-apoptotic function, as disrupting the regulation of the hexokinase-mitochondria association by insulin receptors could trigger photoreceptor apoptosis and retinal degeneration. In this case, treatments that preserve the hexokinase–mitochondria association may serve as a potential therapeutic approach. Interactions HK1 is known to interact with: VDAC, Parkin, EAAT2, Na+/K+ ATPase, and Aconitase.
